articles.title: Dozens of French schools, universities blockaded
articles.excerpt: Students blockaded dozens of high schools and universities across France on Tuesday to maintain pressure on the government over education…
articles.fullText:
Students blockaded dozens of high schools and universities across France on Tuesday to maintain pressure on the government over education reforms as trade unions prepared for a nationwide strike.

After returning from a two-week autumn break, some students resumed their protest campaign Monday, calling on authorities to renovate dilapidated schools, reduce class sizes and create more university places.

Authorities said on Tuesday that 48 out of France's 3,700 high schools were blocked amid tight security, including in Paris, Rennes, and Lyon. The USL student union said 500 establishments were blocked. Fifty-one higher education institutions out of 184 were also disrupted, officials said.

The USL union denounced what it called heavy-handed tactics, with "young people pinned against walls and riot police units deployed" outside schools.

A union representative said authorities appeared to want to blunt a new day of blockades on Thursday when trade unions have called a nationwide strike.

In the northwestern city of Rennes, around 30 students blocked the Brequigny High School, one of the country's largest secondary schools with thousands of students.

Tensions quickly flared between students and a member of the school administration.

"You are not the majority," the staff member protested.

"If we're doing this, it's because everything we've tried before hasn't worked," a student replied.

At a school in the southwestern city of Toulouse, students brandished placards, one saying "Angry, not far right".

In eastern Paris, many teachers at the Voltaire School showed solidarity with students by going on strike to protest at what they called a "massive" police presence outside.

The school protests have fuelled a movement against soaring prices and inadequate public services, which has drawn hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets over the past three weekends and led to some of the worst unrest seen in France in years on October 17. (AFP)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check

A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal.

Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice.

Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave .

—Amit Katwala

Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test

At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.”

One month on, the rebrand is slowly appearing across government websites and documents, but it hasn’t caught on with everyone. Even some of the biggest names in tech still use “AI.”

But the bigger concern is the new term becoming a political loyalty test: Those who use it signal allegiance to the administration. Those who don’t become targets for attacks.

So one month in, who’s on board?

—James O’Donnell

This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Today’s midterms will test AI’s influence on US politics
Candidates are betting that AI regulation will sway voters to their side. ( Axios )
+ Angry constituents could derail Elon Musk’s Republican bets. ( BI )
+ Tech investors are on edge about the results. ( Reuters $)
+ America is divided over AI regulation. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 Nvidia is ordering data centre clients to limit their business with China 
It told providers that the majority of their sales must be non-Chinese. ( FT $)
+ The move follows pressure from Washington. ( Bloomberg $)
+ Chinese AI has ruptured the White House. ( MIT Technology Review )

3 Hackers have turned supermarket fridges into a food security risk
Attacks in Europe have put US supermarket systems on alert. ( CNBC )
+ They’ve also sparked concerns over other domestic appliances. ( BBC )
+ It’s a good time for doing crime. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Scientists have detected signals at the smallest scale ever explored
The discovery offers clues to a world of exotic new particles. ( BBC )
+ It came via CERN’s Large Hadron Collider. ( The Times $)

5 Zapping part of the brain makes you think harder—at a cost
It can both improve performance and reduce motivation. ( New Scientist $)
+ Neuropixels probes are transforming how we study the brain. ( Nature )

6 Big tech is splurging on mega gas plants to power data centers
The projectsthreaten to reverse years of climate pledges. ( WP $)

7 Google says an Android partner infected 1.3 million devices
The malware infected TV boxes and other Android-based devices. ( Verge )

8 Apple is trying to create its first robot
It’s proving a lot harder than expected, though. ( Information $)
+ AI robots are still a long way from useful. ( MIT Technology Review )

9 China’s biggest shopping festival has a new product to sell: AI
AI tokens have become a major new Singles’ Day category. ( Reuters $)

10 A meteorite in the Sahara has revealed new clues about Mars
Its chemistry may help explain how the planet lost its water. ( Wired $)

Quote of the day

“Don’t spend money unduly by asking a human expert to enter into a debate with a robot expert.”

—Steven Benmor, a family lawyer, tells the Wall Street Journal that clients increasingly need to pay human experts to correct advice they’ve received from chatbots.

One more thing

The noise we make is hurting animals. Can we learn to shut up?

As human society has expanded, animals have started struggling to hear one another. For many birds, the noise has grown so loud that they’ve begun to sing with faster trills. Now, their mating calls aren’t as effective.

The growing hubbub can also increase bird-on-bird conflict, and entire species that can’t handle urban clamor simply leave town for good. But there are technological solutions to the noises hurting animals—and they could help humans, too.

Read the full story .

—Clive Thompson

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ Watch five newborn cheetah cubs grow up on the Smithsonian’s livestream.
+ Fifty years after Songs in the Key of Life , Stevie Wonder has released four lost tracks from the album.
+ 50 air guitarists shredded absolutely nothing at the 30th Air Guitar World Championships in Finland.
+ The Ocean Photographer of the Year winners show both the beauty of marine life and the perils it faces.

articles.title: HK recovery uneven despite high GDP: economist
articles.excerpt: A local economist said Hong Kong’s third-quarter GDP performance has lifted business sentiment, but the recovery remains uneven and will…
articles.fullText:
A local economist said Hong Kong’s third-quarter GDP performance has lifted business sentiment, but the recovery remains uneven and will take time to broaden.

Ho Lok-sang, adjunct professor with the Academy for Applied Policy Studies and Education Futures at the Education University of Hong Kong, made the assessment as advance estimates showed Hong Kong’s economy grew 5.2 percent year on year in the third quarter of 2026.

The clearest sign of recovery, he said, was in prime office space.

"Especially for the Grade A centrally located locations, [the] office take-up rate is pretty impressive," he said. "Now, certainly it’s recovering."

But Ho stressed that the strength is not spreading beyond that segment.

"On the outside of the Grade A and centrally located areas, office demand is still relatively weak, and the demand for commercial properties is still relatively weak," he said.

He added that a broader recovery will not come quickly and will likely depend on lower rents.

"I think that it will take quite some time to recover, and I think recovery will also necessitate a decline in rents," Ho said.

Ho was more upbeat about the rest of the year's outlook.

"Definitely the full year growth is going to be quite strong, and I am pretty confident that it will be over four percent or could be as much as 4.5 percent,” he said.

The government's real GDP growth forecast for 2026 as a whole is 3.5 to 4.5 percent.

Ho said the financial sector is performing "pretty well, extremely well", with IPOs still at a very high level and "no sign of it ebbing".

He added that exports, too, are "doing quite well".

But he flagged persistent weak spots: "Demand in terms of both construction demand and also the retail consumption demand and restaurant business are still lagging behind".

To support these sectors, Ho pointed to major events and tourism.

"Of course the major events – for example concerts and Halloween and so on – it’s entirely possible to boost tourism even more," he said.

"Tourism is doing pretty well this year, and we hope that the tourists can stay a bit longer and consume a bit more."

Ho said that outcome depends on the business sector and the government continuing to promote such major events.

Meanwhile, Kenny Shui, vice president of Our Hong Kong Foundation, said the third-quarter figures pointed to strengthening momentum: goods exports rose 30.4 percent on AI and electronics demand, while services exports grew 4.3 percent on tourism and financial activity.

But he said private consumption rose just 2.8 percent, slower than the previous quarter, showing that the strength in retail and investment has yet to fully reach households.

"Growth momentum is broadening, but the recovery still needs to be felt more widely," Shui said.

With first-nine-month growth at 5.1 percent, Shui expects a fourth-quarter growth of four to five percent and full-year growth of around five percent – above the government’s forecast, leaving room for an upward revision.

He cautioned, however, that interest rates could weigh on business investment and household spending, and with unemployment at 3.9 percent, consumption still needs job and income support.

In the fourth quarter, the key will be whether exports stay strong and consumption and employment improve, Shui added.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: HK takes five of top 10 in QS Asia university rankings
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong has dominated the QS Asia University Rankings 2027, with five of the city’s institutions placing in the top…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong has dominated the QS Asia University Rankings 2027, with five of the city’s institutions placing in the top 10.

The University of Hong Kong (HKU) retained the top spot, while City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) rose to fourth and the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) climbed to fifth.

CityUHK and CUHK had tied for seventh a year earlier.

The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU) and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) shared ninth place.

The rankings, compiled by international higher education experts at QS, assessed more than 1,700 universities across 26 higher education systems.

Ben Sowter, QS' senior vice-president, said Hong Kong continues to set the benchmark for university performance in Asia.

"The University of Hong Kong leads the region for a second consecutive year, and having five Hong Kong institutions in the top 10, more than any other higher education system, is an exceptional achievement," he said.

"Increasing international engagement and growing recognition among academics and employers reinforce Hong Kong's regional strength, at a time when competition for students, researchers and academic talent is intensifying across Asia."

Xiang Zhang, president and vice-chancellor of HKU, attributed the university’s second straight top ranking in Asia to its community’s unwavering commitment to academic excellence and its recent drive for change.

"We will continue to draw the world’s finest minds to shape an academic ecosystem driven by a spirit of inquiry, propelling Hong Kong’s advancement as an international hub for education, innovation and technology, while supporting the nation's high-quality development through scientific breakthroughs and contributing to solving global challenges," he said in a statement.

Meanwhile, CityUHK acting president Lee Chun-sing described the university’s rise into the top five for the first time as an encouraging achievement.

"This progress reflects the collective efforts of our academic community to pursue excellence in research and create an inspiring learning environment," Lee said in a statement.

"It also demonstrates the success of our strategic commitment to recruiting global academic talent and nurturing future leaders."

The top 10 also included three mainland institutions – among them Peking University and Tsinghua University – and two universities from Singapore.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Spanish footballer dies after collision with keeper
articles.excerpt: Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died on Tuesday as a result of injuries he suffered in a sickening collision with…
articles.fullText:
Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died on Tuesday as a result of injuries he suffered in a sickening collision with FC Andorra's goalkeeper in a Spanish second division match.

"Broken with pain, with a lump in our throat and unable to believe this is real, CD Tenerife announces the tragic death...of Jesus de Miguel Alameda," his club Tenerife said in a statement.

"No words can ease the pain, nothing can lessen this great feeling of sadness. Our thoughts are with the family, his close friends and Tenerife fans, who today are grieving over this terrible news."

De Miguel, 30, was fouled in the middle of the pitch by Equatorial Guinea international goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who had raced out of his goal.

The incident happened towards the end of the match, which was tied at 2-2. Owono was sent off and the match was subsequently abandoned.

Spanish media said that De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest and was resuscitated, with Tenerife later saying the player's condition had "worsened neurologically", before his death.

De Miguel had been at Tenerife for just over a season, having joined in the summer of 2025 from Castellon.

"I am so deeply sorry. Rest in peace, Jesus," former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, Andorra's majority shareholder, wrote on social media.

Andorra also sent their "most sincere condolences" to De Miguel's family, team-mates and Tenerife.

Real Madrid, Barcelona, Atletico Madrid and other clubs in Spain also sent messages of condolence, as well as the Spanish football federation.

"Shattered by this sad news, the Royal Spanish Football Federation wishes to express our deepest sorrow at his passing today," wrote the federation in a statement. (AFP)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
articles.excerpt: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them…
articles.fullText:
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.

Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code.

The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators .

Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.

An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.

In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.

A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).

Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.

The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.

A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”

Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.

During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.

There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.

Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.

Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.”

One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.

It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.

“Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior.

Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.)

Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?

“It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine talks set for Abu Dhabi next week
articles.excerpt: The Kremlin confirmed on Tuesday that US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks to end more than four years of war will take place…
articles.fullText:
The Kremlin confirmed on Tuesday that US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks to end more than four years of war will take place in Abu Dhabi next week.

US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff earlier announced the meeting will take place on November 10-11.

Witkoff met with both Russia's Vladimir Putin and Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky last month, with all sides announcing three-way talks will resume in November, as Washington pushes an end to the dragging Ukraine-Russia war.

"The Russian delegation will arrive on November 10-11 in Abu Dhabi to take part in trilateral talks," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters, including AFP.

The Russian delegation will be led by Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who took part in previous negotiations that failed to reach a breakthrough.

Medinsky, who is 56 and previously served as culture minister, is known for his nationalistic views on Russian history.

He took part in failed 2022 talks between Russia and Ukraine at the start of the war, also leading the Russian delegation in Istanbul last year and in Geneva earlier this year.

Medinsky, who was born in Ukraine, has co-authored Russian history school textbooks praising Moscow's role in Ukraine. (AFP)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Collaboration is key to development, Nobel winner says
articles.excerpt: An Australian astronomer and Nobel laureate has called on fellow researchers to share their results and foster collaboration, in line…
articles.fullText:
An Australian astronomer and Nobel laureate has called on fellow researchers to share their results and foster collaboration, in line with the spirit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) to break down barriers.

World leaders are expected to gather in Shenzhen later this month for the Apec Economic Leaders' Meeting. China, as host member nation, has outlined three core priorities: openness, innovation, and cooperation.

Those are also values that Brian Schmidt has been advocating for years.

An astrophysicist by profession, he won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011 for the discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe.

Schmidt then became vice-chancellor of the Australian National University in 2016. During his eight-year tenure, he discovered the importance of having a suitable environment for students to turn their concepts into tangible results.

He said Shenzhen is the place to be for researchers.

"I'm from Canberra in Australia. There is almost certainly not going to be the pieces in Canberra for me to say, 'I've got this idea, let me take and make a prototype'," he told Shenzhen Media Group in an interview.

"And Shenzhen, every one of those pieces is there – the drone manufacturer, I need a camera manufacturer, I need an AI integrator, and I can just kind of go through and put it together.

"Which means that developing an idea into a prototype, you can do just phenomenally fast in Shenzhen compared to literally any place in the world."

While Shenzhen offers the ingredients to accelerate scientific development, Schmidt says the people involved in it must be willing to share their knowledge for the research community to thrive.

"It's really easy to start saying all this basic research is really valuable; therefore we don't share it. But that means that we all have to reinvent it, we don't get to work together, we don't get to know each other, and the whole thing just kind of... no one ends up with anything," he explained.

He encouraged researchers to collaborate, especially at a time when countries and blocs are drawing up trade barriers.

"Because there's many, many barriers going up right now. So Apec is trying to lower those barriers. So it's really important that we keep focusing on that, because if we focus [on] how, you know, you might take my idea, and I might take your idea, then we don't work together."

At a recent forum in Beijing, Schmidt also urged scientists to cooperate wherever they could to solve global sustainability issues.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Hong Kong economy grew 5.2pc in Q3 2026
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong’s economy grew 5.2 percent year on year in the third quarter of 2026, buoyed by stronger exports and…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong’s economy grew 5.2 percent year on year in the third quarter of 2026, buoyed by stronger exports and domestic demand, according to advance estimates.

The Census and Statistics Department said the increase compared with a 4.2 percent growth in the second quarter. On a seasonally adjusted basis, GDP rose 1.9 percent quarter on quarter.

For the first nine months combined, the economy grew 5.1 percent – the fastest growth for the period in five years.

Goods exports rose 30.4 percent in real terms, after 28.9 percent in the second quarter, while imports grew 29.9 percent.

Exports of services increased 4.3 percent. Investment strengthened, with gross domestic fixed capital formation up 7.3 percent, while private consumption grew 2.8 percent and government consumption was up 1.7 percent.

A government spokesman said the economy saw robust expansion, underpinned by accelerating exports and solid domestic demand.

He said the outlook remained positive, citing global artificial intelligence investment, inbound tourism, cross-boundary traffic and financial market activity.

But he advised caution over geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and tighter monetary policies by major central banks.

Revised GDP figures and the updated forecast for 2026 will be released on November 13.

Separately, retail sales rose 6.4 percent year on year in September to a provisional HK$33.4 billion – the 17th straight month of expansion.

August’s revised increase was 5.6 percent, and sales for the first nine months were up 8.3 percent by value.

Online sales rose 12 percent to HK$4.4 billion in September, or 13.1 percent of total retail sales, and were up 21.2 percent for the first nine months.

Retail sales volume rose 3.9 percent in September.

The spokesman said solid local consumption sentiment, more visitor arrivals and earlier Mid-Autumn festive sales supported retail growth.

He said upcoming mega events, festive celebrations and inbound tourism should add momentum, though external headwinds warranted close monitoring.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: HK up as policy moves fail to lift mainland markets
articles.excerpt: The mainland's latest effort to steady its sliding stock market struggled for traction on Tuesday, with shares pinned near one-year…
articles.fullText:
The mainland's latest effort to steady its sliding stock market struggled for traction on Tuesday, with shares pinned near one-year lows and investors saying a familiar playbook of encouraging money into the market was falling short this time.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index ended up 132 points, or 0.6 percent, at 23,525 on turnover of HK$236.4 billion.

The tech index rose 28 points, or 0.7 percent, to 3,867 while the China enterprises index was 36 points, or 0.5 percent, higher at 7,943.

Up north, the Shanghai Composite Index fell 29 points, or 0.82 percent, to close at 3,608, on turnover of 810.83 billion yuan.

The Shenzhen Component Index dropped 133 points, or 1.21 percent, to 10,876 on turnover of 892.6 billion while the ChiNext Index plunged 67 points, or 2.73 percent, to 2,391 on turnover of 446.45 billion yuan.

The blue-chip CSI300 is down 13 percent since January.

The index notched its largest monthly fall for a decade in October, led by a slump in AI stocks, and closed 0.2 percent lower on Tuesday.

On Monday regulators responded with measures aimed at funding stock purchases by brokers, funds and companies.

Authorities have also instructed banks to hold off on new listings or large share sales in order to support the market, the Financial Times newspaper reported on Tuesday, citing insiders.

Fund manager Chen Jiande said steps — including central bank swap operations to fund stock purchases and encouraging buybacks — repeated efforts in 2024 and offered a chance to sell, rather than buy.

"These measures were below expectations," said Chen, general manager at Fujian Tianlang Asset Management.

"Many investors in battered tech shares are taking advantage of any rebound to rush out."

UBS economists led by Yu Song agreed that support could build, saying the latest steps marked a new phase of coordinated action across the three main regulators – a sign of commitment to stabilising markets.

But they played down the prospect of a full-scale repeat, arguing economic growth remained within policymakers' comfort zone and the recent selloff did not reflect any fresh deterioration in fundamentals.

In Seoul, the Kospi closed down 210 points, or 3.59 percent, at 5,648 amid chip-sector losses of 4.15 percent for Samsung Electronics and 5.03 percent for SK Hynix. (Reuters/Xinhua)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: 'Joint task force to target bid-rigging early'
articles.excerpt: Secretary for Security Chris Tang on Tuesday said officers from an interdepartmental task force on combating bid-rigging in building maintenance…
articles.fullText:
Secretary for Security Chris Tang on Tuesday said officers from an interdepartmental task force on combating bid-rigging in building maintenance and renovation projects would proactively look for clues to prevent such activities.

Authorities have vowed to step up crackdowns on bid-rigging following the deadly Wang Fuk Court fire.

Proposed measures included the criminalisation of bid-rigging in relation to these projects, enabling a dual-track approach of both criminal and civil enforcement.

Authorities will also set up a joint task force that comprises officers from police, the ICAC and the Competition Commission to better coordinate law enforcement actions.

Speaking to lawmakers at a meeting of the Legislative Council’s Panel on Security and Panel on Economic Development, Tang said the task force's establishment could enable early intervention.

Tang said officers would adopt different tactics against bid-rigging, such as surveillance, undercover operations and the use of informants.

He added that the three agencies of the task force would also attend owners’ corporation meetings to look for suspicious activities, including people who hold many proxy votes or suspected triad members engaging in harassment or intimidation.

Officers would take enforcement actions when necessary, he added.

“If we notice any abnormal situations at the scene that violate the law, such as intimidation and blackmail, our law enforcement colleagues on site will take immediate action,” Tang said.

“Even if the situation is not serious enough to require enforcement action, if we notice signs that may point to hidden crimes, we will carry out investigations.”

Tang said the task force would consider a series of factors when deciding which projects would be prioritised for investigation.

“We will consider the impact of the projects, for example, projects conducted at large estates with a lot of residents and those involving a large amount of money, and if someone seeking to participate in bid-rigging has triad backgrounds – these are all factors we take into consideration.”

Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau, meanwhile, told lawmakers that relevant legislative amendments to combat bid-rigging would be submitted to the legislature as soon as possible.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Mideast conflict forces postponement of Asian Cup
articles.excerpt: The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has postponed the 2027 Asian Cup by almost a year because of the conflict in…
articles.fullText:
The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has postponed the 2027 Asian Cup by almost a year because of the conflict in the Middle East and recent deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.

The AFC issued a statement on Tuesday saying after extensive consultations with Saudi organisers it had decided to push the tournament kickoff back from January 7 to December 23.

The organising committee “approved to reschedule the flagship national team tournament in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions,” the AFC said in a statement.

“Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organisation and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders.”

The new dates — December 23, 2027 to January 21, 2028 — will be submitted to Fifa for approval.

The decision to delay the tournament ends months of speculation about a postponement which, until recently, had been rejected by local organisers.

As recently as last week, Saudi officials released the kickoff times and finalised schedule for the 2027 tournament in a move aimed at assuring continental football federations that planning was on track.

Muhammed Q. Alghamdi, a spokesman for the organising committee, last month told members at an Asian Football Confederation meeting in Tokyo that “daily life is ongoing in Saudi Arabia,” despite the regional hostilities.

Before that meeting, AFC President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa had indicated that the Asian Cup could be postponed by a year if necessary, saying “we can wait until the end of November” to make a decision.”

The month-long tournament was scheduled to feature 24 teams playing matches in eight venues across three cites — Riyadh, Jeddah, and Khobar.

Iran qualified and has been grouped with Syria, China and Kyrgyzstan for the league stage.

Asia's marquee continental club tournament — the AFC Champions League Elite — has been disrupted by the conflict.

A game between Cristiano Ronaldo ’s Al-Nassr and Uzbekistan’s Neftchi Fergana was delayed on October 12 after Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence issued a security alert.

An Al-Nassr’s home game in Riyadh last week against Al-Wasl of the United Arab Emirates was postponed because the visiting team didn't travel.

Among other major sports events that have been moved or cancelled in Saudi are the WTA Finals, the season-ending event in women’s tennis, which moved from Riyadh to Indian Wells, California. (AP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: HK eager to help build 'enterprises of tomorrow'
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong is ambitious about helping create the "enterprises of tomorrow", Financial Secretary Paul Chan said on Tuesday in amplifying…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong is ambitious about helping create the "enterprises of tomorrow", Financial Secretary Paul Chan said on Tuesday in amplifying the pivotal role the Northern Metropolis would play in realising this vision.

That came as he told investors at the Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit in Central about the dedication that investors can expect of Hong Kong to strengthening its contribution to innovation.

“Our ambition is not only to finance businesses created elsewhere, but also to help create the enterprises of tomorrow,” Chan said.

“The Northern Metropolis is central to this effort.

"It will bring universities, research facilities and technology enterprises closer together, linking education, technology and talent more closely with industry.”

The mega development project in the northern New Territories would, Chan said, serve as a base for closer ties with other Greater Bay Area cities, allowing Hong Kong to draw on their strengths in commercialisation, engineering and advanced manufacturing.

Hong Kong was eager to pair promising businesses with capital and partners, as well as give investors trusted pathways into unfamiliar sectors and economies, he added.

Hong Kong had, Chan pointed out, also taken steps to widen its connections with various economies and broaden asset classes in various regions.

“In Southeast Asia, we are welcoming more enterprises from Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia to lease in Hong Kong,” he said.

“In the Middle East, Hong Kong and Saudi Arabia have listed ETFs, tracking each other's markets, giving investors new routes to invest.”

“In Central Asia, Kazakhstan has already tapped Hong Kong's equity and bond markets. We welcome more issuers to raise capital here through listings and bond issuances.”

Chan added that Hong Kong would also continue to expand the range of assets and financial services to give investors more options to diversify.

This, he said, included a central focus on developing a commodity and gold trading ecosystem.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Real estate recovery drives growth forecast higher: FS
articles.excerpt: Financial Secretary Paul Chan on Tuesday said all three drivers of economic growth performed well in the third quarter, with…
articles.fullText:
Financial Secretary Paul Chan on Tuesday said all three drivers of economic growth performed well in the third quarter, with consumption, investment, and exports all recording growth to varying degrees.

Hong Kong's advance estimates for the third-quarter GDP are set to be released later in the day.

The financial chief had announced over the weekend that the city's full-year economic growth forecast will be revised upwards following a stronger-than-expected 5.1 percent GDP growth in the first half of the year.

Chan said other factors also supported the projection, noting that full-year visitor arrivals are likely to exceed the target of 50 million and that the real estate market is improving.

"The residential property market has been on the rise since the latter half of last year. Last year, the increase was approximately three percent, while the rise this year has been between seven and 10 percent. In the residential property market, it's fair to say we are moving into a stage of steady ascent.” he said.

"In commercial real estate, we have observed significant improvements in office rentals, in terms of rental prices and vacancy rates, particularly in central business districts. It has also stabilised in other districts."

An expected influx of visitors towards the end of the year will also have a positive impact on the retail and catering sectors, Chan added.

While certain industries, such as construction, catering, and retail, are facing more pressure with higher jobless rates, Chan stressed that the overall employment situation is stable, with unemployment standing at around 3.9 percent.

In predicting next year’s economic growth, Chan stressed that government economists are currently assessing the impact of several key factors.

These, he said, include expected high interest rates, geopolitical uncertainties like fluctuating oil prices driven by Middle East wars, upcoming elections in major economies, and the reallocation of international funds.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Financial institutions laud HK's gateway guardianship
articles.excerpt: Global bank leaders have lauded Hong Kong for its role as a gateway between the mainland and the rest of…
articles.fullText:
Global bank leaders have lauded Hong Kong for its role as a gateway between the mainland and the rest of the world, facilitating two-way financial flows and minimising risks in an era of uncertainty.

At a panel meeting held at the Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Central, State Street chairman and chief executive Ronald O’Hanley noted that trade patterns had changed in recent years due to uncertainties brought by the pandemic and global conflicts.

More borrowers and people looking to raise capital, he said, are looking for safer options when building supply chains and structuring financing – switching from “just in time to just in case”.

“Where we’re seeing the most change is around the role of China, and Hong Kong is the gateway to that,” O’Hanley said.

"It’s the kind of movement of money north and south and movement of capital north and south, and Hong Kong is playing that role.”

Barclays group chief executive C S Venkatakrishnan said firms had been reducing their dependency on strategic imports over the past decade and that the city which is positioned as both an international financial centre as well as a domestic one is the one that can help countries manage the dependencies.

“I think in order for international finance not to get caught up in the strategic breakdown of dependence, it’s important for the international financial centres like Hong Kong to do what you’re doing – which is to have fair and transparent regulation to promote growth and to make it easy for people to operate,” he said.

BNP Paribas chairman Jean Lemierre noted that more mainland firms were operating in Europe.

With Hong Kong being a renminbi hub, it acts as a bridge between China and Europe that helps these companies gain access to the euro, he said, adding that mainland firms can have better understanding of the European market through the SAR.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Patience pays off at Melbourne Cup for Point Of Law
articles.excerpt: Point Of Law ran down surprise leader Royal Supremacy on the home straight to win the 166th running of the…
articles.fullText:
Point Of Law ran down surprise leader Royal Supremacy on the home straight to win the 166th running of the Melbourne Cup at Flemington on Tuesday, giving trainer Ciaron Maher his second victory in Australia's biggest horse race.

The four-year-old stallion bided his time for the first 2,900 metres as rank outsider Royal Supremacy opened up a lead of 20 lengths but exploded off the final corner and sprinted home to win the A$10.2 million handicap by two lengths.

"Please don't wake me up, it's an amazing feeling," jockey Ethan Brown said from the saddle as he brought the 6-1 second favourite in.

"I looked up and Royal Supremacy was about 20 in front. I thought, 'oh, God, just stay cool, stay patient, cut the bend'. And once he got that clear running, his turn of foot was enormous. He's going to be a superstar horse if he isn't already."

Zahrann finished second ahead of Juja Kibo to give Maher, who co-trained 2022 winner Gold Trip and had seven horses in the race, a sweep of the top three.

Irish trainer Joseph O'Brien prepared five horses for the race but had to settle for a best finish of fourth place through Sons and Lovers.

Favourite Hopewell Rock finished ninth, while Royal Supremacy's reward for leading for most of the race was fifth place.

Jockey Brown left his home in Alice Springs in Australia's remote Northern Territory as a teenager to chase his dream and spent six months out of the sport after a nasty fall at Flemington three years ago.

"I was inches from losing my life, but a bit of time off and I realised I wasn't any good at anything else," he said.

"There was a slow burn inside of me."

The 27-year-old paid tribute to the trust Maher had placed in him by giving him the ride.

"He's one of many people, but he's believed in me. He showed that by putting me on."

Maher returned the compliment during the post-race ceremony.

"I could just see how dedicated he was this year," said the former jockey, who has made a success of importing horses to train and race in Australia.

"He was dialled in and that was a beautiful exhibition of how to ride a horse in the Melbourne Cup."

Earlier, Asterix was scratched and trainer Chris Waller fined A$50,000 hours before the race after a stablehand applied a liniment to the gelding's forelegs without permission from the stewards. (Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Beijing approves removal of Winnie Ho as housing chief
articles.excerpt: The State Council has decided to remove Winnie Ho from the post of housing secretary of the Hong Kong government…
articles.fullText:
The State Council has decided to remove Winnie Ho from the post of housing secretary of the Hong Kong government, Xinhua reported on Tuesday.

It said the decision, made on Tuesday, was in accordance with the Basic Law and based on the suggestion of Chief Executive John Lee.

That came after Lee said Ho had tendered her resignation on October 28 and indicated that she would shoulder political accountability for the Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po.

A day after that, the government made public the investigation report by an independent committee into the deadly blaze and unveiled sweeping measures to prevent a recurrence.

In a statement, Lee recounted Ho's career from the time that she joined the government in 1992, becoming director of architectural services in 2020 to being appointed as secretary for housing in 2022.

Lee said Ho had been dedicated to implementing his directives, including constructing some 30,000 Light Public Housing units, shortening the composite waiting time for subsidised rental housing from 6.1 years to 4.8 years, effectively combating the abuse of public rental housing and enacting the Basic Housing Units Ordinance to eradicate substandard subdivided units.

"As she officially leaves her post today, I wish her all the best in her future endeavours and a healthy life," he said.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Parking meters restored after hours of breakdown
articles.excerpt: The Transport Department said the operation of the city's parking meter system had returned to normal following emergency repairs after…
articles.fullText:
The Transport Department said the operation of the city's parking meter system had returned to normal following emergency repairs after a breakdown that lasted for nearly four hours on Tuesday morning.

The department said it received a report from the operator at about 8.20am that the system had malfunctioned.

The Digital Policy Office was notified of the incident, the department said, noting that there was no evidence to suggest the system had been hacked.

Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said officials had urged the operator of the parking meters to submit a report as soon as possible.

"I want to reiterate that we attach huge importance to this incident and the system malfunction. I have instructed the Transport Department to require the system operator, HKT, to submit a report as soon as possible. I hope an initial report can be submitted within the next 24 hours," she said.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: New service to simplify mainland flight transit in HK
articles.excerpt: Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan on Tuesday said a new service had been launched to streamline international travel…
articles.fullText:
Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan on Tuesday said a new service had been launched to streamline international travel for mainland passengers departing from regional airports via Hong Kong International Airport to destinations around the world.

A pilot phase is underway in collaboration with airports in Hangzhou and Wuhan.

The new initiative is part of the national aviation programme named: "Trunk-Branch Connectivity, Whole-Network Linkage".

Passengers can check in for their entire journey at their local airports, and fly out to international destinations via Hong Kong, instead of having to re-claim their luggage and then check in again in the SAR.

Speaking at the opening ceremony of this year's Super Terminal Expo, Chan described the scheme as a game-changing service.

"To put this into perspective, this transfer platform is already active across more than 260 airports in the mainland and has accumulatively facilitated over 260 million transfer passengers, allowing tens of millions of travellers to enjoy the unprecedented convenience of one-stop check-in and seamless baggage transfers," she said.

"This is far more than a commercial expansion. It is a policy breakthrough, which embeds Hong Kong directly into the national overall aviation architecture."

Chan stressed that Hong Kong International Airport plays a vital “linchpin role” to fulfil the SAR’s unique mandate as a super-connector and a super value-adder that bridges the country and the world.

Enhancing connectivity between the world’s second-largest economy and the rest of the world, she said, also unlocks tremendous opportunities for trade and aviation.

To facilitate this goal, Chan noted that Hong Kong had also set a target of expanding its global aviation network from the existing 220 destinations to 240 under its recently unveiled five-year plan.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
articles.excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox…
articles.fullText:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first,  sign up here .

At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.

Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).

The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.

It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).

But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.

So one month in, who’s on board?

Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period.

There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.

The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents).

As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.

But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too.

In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.

But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.

Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia.

But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.

In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.

Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too .

One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order , leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month. 

But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.

People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change.

If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. It’s easy to imagine that two people chatting about, say, whether chatbots are good or bad for our mental health will stop once they realize one of them is saying “super intelligence” and the other “AI.” That would be a shame for us all.

Midterm elections are tomorrow. Americans say AI is more important to them in this election than environmental and climate policy (and Democrats even rank it above abortion and gun policy). We’re only just beginning to have a national conversation about what AI will mean for our lives. Whether or not “Super Intelligence” catches on, turning the terminology itself into a loyalty test will do nothing to advance a national conversation about AI that’s only just getting started.

articles.title: HK blueprint 'gives investors the certainty they seek'
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong can offer certainty, clarity and confidence to global investors at a time when structural forces are rewriting the…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong can offer certainty, clarity and confidence to global investors at a time when structural forces are rewriting the rules of global finance, Chief Executive John Lee said on Tuesday.

He was speaking in Central at the Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit, which gathered some 280 of the sector's leaders from around the world.

While blockchain and tokenisation were rebuilding the world's financial infrastructure, and AI was reshaping productivity, labour markets and competition, Lee noted that Hong Kong’s first five-year blueprint had set out clear developmental directions.

“The plan delivers what markets value most: certainty,” he said.

“In an era of ever-shifting terrain, it lays out a transparent roadmap, showing where Hong Kong is heading and how we intend to get there. I invite you to consider that roadmap yours as well.

“And to be clear, as we rethink the playbook, as we create strategic blueprints for Hong Kong's development, we ensure the value proposition of our city remains intact – that is our competitive edge under the ‘One Country, Two Systems’ principle.”

Lee added that he would be attending the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen this month with the goal of advancing regional economic cooperation.

Meanwhile, Vice Premier He Lifeng said Hong Kong’s development had always been in sync with the nation, adding that ensuring the sound development of the SAR had been a key strategic consideration of the central government.

Delivering a speech to summit through video, he urged the SAR to leverage its advantages under "One Country, Two Systems".

"Further demonstrating its international characteristics, Hong Kong will continuously deepen and expand exchanges and cooperation with the world in areas such as the economy, technology, and culture," He said.

"It will provide greater convenience and better opportunities for more international capital, institutions, and talent to come to Hong Kong for entrepreneurship and development.

"We will, as always, fully support Hong Kong in maintaining its unique status and advantages over the long term, build a higher-level, more competitive free and open economic environment, and create broader space for future development."

He also expressed the central government’s confidence in the SAR’s five-year blueprint to develop Hong Kong.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Trump California gambit gets short shrift in top court
articles.excerpt: The US Supreme Court has rejected a Trump administration emergency attempt to force California to set aside the mail-in ballots…
articles.fullText:
The US Supreme Court has rejected a Trump administration emergency attempt to force California to set aside the mail-in ballots of more than 20,000 people on the grounds they may not be American citizens.

Acting a day before the US midterm elections, the top court denied the request in an unsigned, one-sentence ruling, as is common in urgent cases before the court.

It gave no reasoning for the decision.

The federal government had accused California of having 190,000 illegal voters on its rolls.

It recently revised the figure to 20,000 and filed an emergency lawsuit – after early voting had begun – to stop the state from sending ballots to them.

The Supreme Court action came after lower courts last week – and again on Monday – rejected the demand by the US Department of Justice, with one judge calling it brazen pre-election interference.

Solicitor General D John Sauer, in an emergency filing with the Supreme Court, had said that "once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back".

The California ballot case appeared to be another attempt by the administration to cast doubt on the results of Tuesday's vote, in which US President Donald Trump's Republican Party is at risk of losing control of Congress.

US District Judge David Carter last week refused to order the seizure of the ballots and sided with the government of Democratic-led California.

"The DOJ's actions are indicative of a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials," Carter said.

Another district judge, James Boasberg, also ruled against the Trump administration on Monday, saying the lists of alleged non-citizens were "flawed".

A controversy similar to California's arose in neighbouring Nevada.

The administration said initially it had identified 16,000 non-citizen voters there, but after verification procedures that number dropped to 185 – and then to zero.

Studies repeatedly show that while cases of voter fraud exist, such incidents are extremely rare and do not influence election results.

In another closely-watched election case, a federal judge in Alaska over the weekend tossed out a bid by the Trump administration to hold up US Senate election results in the state should the Democratic candidate win.

The DOJ had asked the court to block certification of the results if Republican Dan Sullivan, the incumbent, loses on Tuesday because a second candidate, also named Dan Sullivan, would have siphoned off votes.

Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Alaska, has denied recruiting the second Sullivan into the race, but The New York Times reported that members of her campaign staff had been involved. (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Analysts: China could erode Taiwan’s hold on remote Pratas Island without invasion
articles.excerpt: Restricting supplies could give Beijing leverage, but forcing a withdrawal would risk a wider crisis.
articles.fullText:
China could cut off supplies to Taiwan-controlled Pratas Island, but forcing Taipei to abandon the remote outpost would require a sustained operation that might be too risky for Beijing, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
The tiny atoll known as Dongsha Island in Chinese lies more than 400 kilometers (250 miles) from Taiwan’s main island, about 260 kilometers (160 miles) from the Chinese mainland in the northern South China Sea.
The island’s isolation makes maintaining access by sea and air central to sustaining the coast guard and military personnel stationed there.
Beijing likely has the power to cut Pratas off completely, but such a move might not be necessary at all, Benjamin Blandin, a maritime security expert and visiting research fellow at Taiwan’s Institute for National Defense and Security Research, told RFA.
“China could achieve significant strategic benefits without imposing a complete blockade or forcing an immediate Taiwanese withdrawal,” said Blandin.
For Beijing, the potential gains could include regulating selected activities or compelling Taiwan to negotiate access, Blandin said. Such restrictions could erode Taipei’s authority even while Taiwanese personnel remained on the island.
A map showing the location of Taiwan-controlled Pratas Island in the northern South China Sea.
(RFA) But disrupting deliveries and making the outpost impossible to sustain are different objectives, Sylwia M. Gorska, a doctoral candidate in international relations at Britain’s University of Central Lancashire, told RFA.
“Making Taiwan’s presence unsustainable would require much more extensive restrictions, particularly given the island’s existing air and maritime supply options,” Gorska told RFA.
The portion of the atoll above sea level features an air strip and two piers.
Both analysts cautioned that recent encounters near Pratas do not establish that Beijing has decided to cut the island off, though these encounters have sharpened concerns about access.
Posturing coast guards
Taiwan’s coast guard on Sunday accused China of “harassment” after a Chinese coast guard ship on Saturday went into a restricted area of water near the atoll. A Taiwan coast guard vessel got as close as 1 nautical mile and asked the Chinese ship to leave.
Taipei called on China to “immediately cease” its acts of harassment, after what it said was the 13th such incursion near Pratas Island this year.
China maintains that the atoll is within its sovereign territory and called the incident a “routine law enforcement patrol.”
It was the third Pratas-related incident between the two countries in October alone, with similar incidents occurring Oct. 18 and Oct. 1.
A Taiwan coast guard patrol vessel, right, sailing near a China coast guard ship in waters south of Kinmen, Taiwan, July 8, 2026.
(Taiwan Coast Guard/AFP) Such encounters challenge Taiwan’s authority, the analysts said, but the more consequential test would involve Chinese ships issuing instructions to Taiwanese supply missions, then enforcing compliance.
Blandin identified three potentially overlapping stages: normalizing China’s maritime presence, asserting jurisdiction, and establishing effective control over access.
Demands for identification, inspections or course changes would indicate a move toward exercising authority, he said, adding that repeated obstruction of deliveries, personnel rotations or emergency evacuations would provide stronger evidence of an isolation campaign.
“The distinction between challenging Taiwan’s maritime authority and actively preventing the replenishment of its outposts is fundamental,” Blandin said.
Gorska said requirements for advance authorization or compulsory inspections would signal an attempt to regulate access. Persistent obstruction of successive deliveries, particularly alongside interference with flights, would indicate a more extensive effort to isolate Pratas.
“The principal concern is that Beijing may eventually seek to enforce the authority it is currently asserting, thereby transforming jurisdictional claims into restrictions on access,” she said.
Keeping supplies moving
Taiwan has strengthened its local patrol capabilities. Its coast guard said in September that a wharf renovation had been completed on July 1, allowing newly built 100-ton patrol boats to be stationed at Pratas alongside regular deployments of larger patrol ships nearby.
Those improvements strengthen the response around the atoll but do not guarantee security along its supply routes, Gorska said.
Larger reserves would give Taiwan more time to respond to disrupted deliveries, while maintaining maritime and air transport would provide flexibility. Blandin said sea transport would remain important for substantial quantities of equipment and provisions, with aircraft offering a complementary option when conditions permitted.
The outpost at Pratas atoll, as of Oct. 4, 2020. China has flown near this Taiwanese-occupied feature in the South China Sea over 200 times with military aircraft this year, including with surveillance planes and anti-submarine warfare planes.
(Planet Labs) Escorting deliveries could help preserve access, but repeated Chinese obstructions would force difficult decisions about how far Taiwan should go to challenge them.
Taipei could deploy additional coast guard vessels, improve surveillance or involve military assets more directly, Blandin said. Each option would have to be weighed against the risk of escalation.
“Beijing’s main challenge would be sustaining those restrictions without losing control over the level of confrontation,” Gorska said.
Stopping an individual delivery leaves room to retreat or negotiate, she said. Repeatedly preventing escorted ships or aircraft from reaching Pratas would carry substantially greater risks and could provoke a wider cross-Strait crisis.
Lessons from the Philippines
The Philippines’ efforts to supply its outpost aboard the grounded BRP Sierra Madre at Second Thomas Shoal offer a comparison, although the geography, logistical needs and security arrangements differ.
Blandin said Manila’s persistence in continuing deliveries, along with documenting and publicizing confrontations, offered lessons for Taiwan. Defensive equipment, surveillance and proportionate responses could improve resilience, but none would guarantee access against sustained interference.
Gorska said practical arrangements to prevent dangerous encounters also carried a political challenge: communication should not become an acceptance of Beijing’s claimed authority to approve deliveries.
A Taiwanese coast guard handles a machine gun at a fort on the Pratas Islands in the South China Sea in a file photo from January 2000.
(Reuters) The comparison has another major limit. The Philippines has a mutual defense treaty with Washington, and U.S. defense guidelines explicitly include armed attacks on Philippine coast guard vessels in the South China Sea within those commitments. Taiwan has no equivalent treaty.
The Taiwan Relations Act treats efforts to determine Taiwan’s future through nonpeaceful means, including boycotts or embargoes, as a matter of grave concern to the United States. It does not specify a U.S. military response to interference with supplies to Pratas.
That uncertainty would factor into Beijing’s calculations, Gorska said.
For Blandin, China’s ability to deploy ships around Pratas is only the beginning.
“The central question is therefore not simply whether China possesses the capabilities to isolate Pratas, but whether it could sustain such an operation and convert maritime coercion into lasting territorial control at an acceptable political, military and diplomatic cost.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: HK stocks buck regional trend amid midterm jitters
articles.excerpt: Stocks edged generally lower at the start of Asian trade on Tuesday and oil prices stabilised after the previous session's…
articles.fullText:
Stocks edged generally lower at the start of Asian trade on Tuesday and oil prices stabilised after the previous session's tumble, with investors on edge with hours to go to the start of voting for the US midterm elections.

In Hong Kong, however, the benchmark Hang Seng Index opened up 76 points, or 0.33 percent, at 23,469.

The China enterprises index edged up 27 points, or 0.35 percent, to 7,933 while the tech index inched 13 points, or 0.36 percent, higher to 3,853.

Mainland markets went the other way, with the Shanghai Composite Index opening down 13 points, or 0.37 percent, at 3,624.

The Shenzhen Component Index fell 76 points, or 0.69 percent, to 10,934 while the ChiNext Index was 28 points, or 1.18 percent, lower at 2,429.

With the Nikkei closed for a public holiday, the Kospi plunged 143 points, or 2.46 percent, to 5,715 in Seoul and was just a tad worse off at 145 points down at one stage before noon.

"Tuesday will be nothing more than the day ahead of a much bigger day," ING analysts wrote in a note.

By tomorrow, the market will have guidance on the midterm implications and the US Treasury's quarterly refunding announcement, they wrote.

The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was up 2.1 basis points at 4.913 percent.

Overnight, stocks on Wall Street edged lower, with the S&P 500 slipping 0.5 percent as tech-sector earnings weighed on investor confidence, even as data showed US manufacturing activity picked up in October amid strong domestic demand.

Apple shares extended losses, falling 2.8 percent in after-hours trading after the iPhone maker on Monday forecast lower gross margins for the crucial holiday quarter, citing rising memory-chip costs, and projected services revenue growth that fell well short of Wall Street expectations.

Investors are also preparing to vote in the US midterm elections, where President Donald Trump's Republican Party is facing a challenge to keep its hold on Congress.

Opinion polls favour the Democrats to win the House, though the Senate remains too close to call.

Prediction market sites Polymarket and Kalshi currently assign around a 75 percent probability that the Democrats will control the Senate.

"Prediction markets imply the greatest likelihood of a Democratic 'sweep', but polling margins remain broadly comparable to Trump 1.0 midterms in 2018 when Democrats won the House decisively, but Republicans held onto the Senate," MUFG analysts wrote in a note.

"Brazil’s election surprise is a reminder that prediction markets can misprice political tail risks, raising questions around the roughly 70 percent odds now assigned to a blue 'sweep' in the midterms."

Oil prices steadied after a fall, with Brent crude fluctuating between gains and losses and was last 0.1 percent lower at US$104.72 as trading resumed in Asia and investors weighed the state of peace talks between the US and Iran.

The Wall Street Journal on Monday reported the US military struck Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, citing US officials. (Reuters/Xinhua)

articles.title: Parking meters down, emergency repairs under way
articles.excerpt: The Transport Department on Tuesday said that the parking meter system had broken down, with emergency repairs under way. The…
articles.fullText:
The Transport Department on Tuesday said that the parking meter system had broken down, with emergency repairs under way.

The department said it received a report from the operator at about 8.20am that the system had malfunctioned.

It said it instructed the operator to carry out the necessary repairs as soon as possible to minimise the impact on motorists, and to conduct a thorough investigation into the cause of the incident and submit a report.

Motorists with enquiries can call the service hotline at 2332 3700.

Later, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said several parking metres had returned to normal following the repairs.

She added that no parking tickets would be issued until the system was fully restored.

"The Transport Department immediately contacted the police. While the system is being repaired, police will not carry out enforcement on roadside parking spots. People can be sure of that," Chan said.

"I want to reiterate that we attach huge importance to this incident and the system malfunction. I have instructed the Transport Department to require the system operator, HKT, to submit a report as soon as possible. I hope an initial report can be submitted within the next 24 hours."
